strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: existing methods like AVICI fail to scale (OOM) on graphs beyond ~100-200 nodes, while non-amortized methods are prohibitively slow; CauScale demonstrates training on 500-node graphs and inference on 1000-node graphs where prior amortized approaches cannot run.

The two-stream (data + graph) architecture with a data-graph block is a reasonable and well-motivated design that explicitly compresses the data stream while distilling relational information into the graph stream before reduction, mitigating the naive-subsampling concerns raised by the authors.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple axes: varying graph sizes (10 to 1000 nodes), causal mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), in-distribution vs OOD settings, semi-synthetic single-cell GRN data, and sample-size sensitivity analyses, giving a fairly broad picture of behavior.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual components: the reduction unit (time/memory/accuracy trade-off), graph stream/graph prior, tied attention vs vanilla attention, prediction head design, and pooling strategy (average vs max vs strided) — this supports the soundness of individual design choices.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility appendix (data generation procedures, hyperparameters, hardware, training schedule, baseline implementation details), which aids reproducibility even though no code release is explicitly confirmed in the excerpt.

Reports large and consistent speedups (4x-13,000x) alongside strong mAP on many settings, and the efficiency analysis (Section 4.6) provides some theoretical justification for the compute savings from the reduction unit and tied attention.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely a recombination of existing components: tied attention is adopted directly from Rao et al. (2021) (MSA Transformer), the prediction head is adopted from Lippe et al. (2021), and the observation-dimension pooling/reduction is a fairly standard downsampling idea; the main original contribution is the specific two-stream data-graph block design and its coupling to the reduction schedule, which is a comparatively modest architectural contribution.

The comparison to AVICI is potentially unfair/incomplete: AVICI was not retrained on the paper's own training data (using only its pretrained checkpoints) due to reported OOM errors when attempting to train it, while CauScale is trained end-to-end on the same synthetic/GRN datasets used for evaluation; this asymmetry could inflate the apparent accuracy/efficiency gap over AVICI.

Headline efficiency numbers (up to 13,000x speedup) are computed relative to non-amortized methods like NOTEARS, which is an expected and somewhat unsurprising comparison (amortized vs. non-amortized), while comparisons to more comparable amortized baselines (AVICI, SEA) show much smaller (4x-200x) but still meaningful gains; the framing could overstate the practical significance of the largest reported number.

Performance degrades substantially in harder/OOD settings and at scale: e.g., mAP drops to 18.9% for the 1000-node polynomial OOD setting and to 64.5%/79.7% for sigmoid/NN non-additive at 1000 nodes, undermining the headline 99.6%/84.4% mAP figures which correspond to more favorable configurations; the paper could more clearly caveat these headline numbers.

No comparison against other recent amortized/meta-learning causal discovery baselines explicitly discussed in Related Work (e.g., Ke et al. 2023, Dhir et al. 2025), leaving open whether CauScale's gains are specific to the AVICI/SEA comparison set rather than the broader landscape of amortized methods.

Limited statistical rigor: it is unclear whether main synthetic-data results (Table 1) are averaged over multiple random seeds/graph instances with reported variance, unlike the GRN experiments which explicitly average over 5 instances; absence of error bars or significance tests makes it hard to assess robustness of the reported margins over baselines.

Acyclicity is not enforced in the model output, and although this follows prior practice (Lippe et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2025), the paper only reports cycle rates in a limited ablation (Figure 5) rather than as a core evaluation metric across all main experimental settings, leaving the practical validity of predicted DAGs only partially characterized.

The efficiency analysis in Section 4.6 is a simplified theoretical approximation (geometric series assuming B divisible by k) that is validated only against the specific training configuration (B=10, k=2, r=2) rather than empirically verified compute measurements across configurations.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: existing transformer-based approaches (e.g., AVICI) scale poorly in both time and memory as the number of variables grows, and the paper's reduction unit + tied attention weights provide a concrete engineering solution with clear complexity analysis (Section 4.6).

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad: it spans multiple graph topologies (ER, SF, SBM), multiple causal mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), in-distribution and OOD settings, synthetic and semi-synthetic (SERGIO-GRN) data, and graph sizes from 10 to 1000 nodes.

Ablation studies (reduction unit on/off, graph stream/prior removal, tied vs. vanilla attention, prediction head choice, pooling strategy) are informative and help isolate the contribution of individual architectural components.
The reported inference speedups (4x-13,000x) and the ability to train on 500-node graphs where AVICI runs out of memory are a meaningful practical advance if the comparisons are fair.
The paper is generally clearly written with a well-illustrated architecture diagram and reasonably detailed appendix for reproducibility of data generation and baseline settings.
weaknesses: Core architectural ingredients (axial/tied attention from Rao et al. 2021's MSA Transformer, pairwise decomposed prediction head from Lippe et al. 2021, graph-prior injection, two-stream fusion) are largely assembled from existing techniques; the main novel component (the reduction unit) is a relatively simple average-pooling operation, so the overall originality is incremental rather than conceptual.

The comparison with AVICI is potentially unfair and under-explained: because CauScale encounters OOM training on the full dataset without the reduction unit, AVICI is evaluated using an off-the-shelf pretrained checkpoint (scm-v0 / neurips-grn) rather than being retrained on the paper's own training distribution (Appendix C). The catastrophic AVICI accuracy at n=1000 (mAP as low as 0.1-0.9%) is very likely a distribution-mismatch artifact rather than a genuine capability gap, which undermines the headline accuracy and speedup claims against this baseline.

No real-world causal discovery benchmarks are used; all results are on fully synthetic or simulator-generated (SERGIO-GRN) data where ground-truth graphs are known. The causal-sufficiency assumption (no latent confounders) is explicitly adopted, limiting the relevance of the motivating applications (bioinformatics, epidemiology, economics) cited in the introduction.

The efficiency framing is restricted to inference-time cost; the substantial pretraining cost (37+2.75 GPU-hours on 8 GPUs for synthetic data, 44 GPU-hours for GRN data) is not factored into the efficiency analysis or compared against baselines' total cost, which is a significant practical consideration for anyone wanting to reproduce or extend this pretraining pipeline.

Robustness to OOD causal mechanisms is actually weak: mAP drops to 50.3% (n=100) and 18.9% (n=1000) under the polynomial mechanism, and Section 5.5's generalization analysis explicitly notes higher sensitivity to OOD noise/mechanism; this contradicts the abstract's framing of '84.4% on OOD data,' since that figure reflects only the better of the two OOD settings (sigmoid) and masks much weaker polynomial performance.

No variance/error bars or statistical significance testing are reported despite averaging over only 5 independent graph instances per test configuration, making it hard to assess how reliable the reported differences (especially close calls like CauScale vs. SEA-gies on some metrics) actually are.

The graph prior is defined as an inverse covariance matrix, which can be numerically unstable or ill-defined when sample size m is comparable to or smaller than n (e.g., n=1000 experiments use only 1000 samples); this potential numerical issue is not discussed or ablated.

The paper's claim of being 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale' is somewhat overstated given that AVICI, SEA, and Ke et al. 2023 are essentially doing the same amortized pretraining paradigm; the real contribution is efficiency improvement rather than the pretraining paradigm itself.
The project page URL is blank/placeholder and no code repository is linked, raising reproducibility concerns beyond the architectural description provided in the main text and appendix.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important bottleneck: existing amortized causal discovery methods (e.g., AVICI) scale poorly in memory/time with graph size, limiting applicability to large graphs.

The architectural contributions (reduction unit for compressing the sample dimension, tied attention weights, and a two-stream data-graph design that injects statistical priors and relational messages) are reasonable, clearly motivated, and supported by a theoretical efficiency analysis (Section 4.6) showing concrete FLOP and memory reductions.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple axes: varying graph sizes (10 to 1000 nodes), multiple causal mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), in-distribution and OOD generalization, and a semi-synthetic single-cell GRN benchmark, against a fairly comprehensive set of baselines spanning constraint-based, score-based, FCM-based, and amortized paradigms.

Strong quantitative improvements: large mAP gains over baselines in most settings and substantial inference speedups (4x-13,000x), plus successful training at 500-node scale where AVICI reportedly runs out of memory.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of the reduction unit, graph stream/prior, tied attention vs vanilla attention, prediction head design, and pooling strategy, which helps substantiate the design choices.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility appendix covering data generation protocols, baseline implementation settings, and training/hardware configuration.
weaknesses: The project page link is left blank in the abstract ('Our project page is at .'), and no code repository is confirmed as released, which undermines reproducibility given the complexity of the architecture and training pipeline.

The AVICI baseline is evaluated using a pretrained checkpoint rather than being retrained on the same data distribution as CauScale (justified by OOM, but this creates a comparability gap that could partly explain AVICI's unexpectedly poor accuracy in several settings, e.g., near-zero mAP at n=1000).

Performance degrades substantially in harder OOD settings (e.g., 18.9% mAP on polynomial mechanisms at n=1000, and relatively large OA gap vs mAP in several rows), and the OOD noise/mechanism sensitivity noted in Section 5.5 suggests the practical robustness of the method outside the training distribution is still limited; this is only briefly discussed in the generalization analysis without deeper investigation of root causes.

Results on real or genuinely held-out benchmarks (vs. synthetic/semi-synthetic SERGIO-simulated data) are absent, so it remains unclear how well the model's accuracy gains generalize to real causal discovery applications such as bioinformatics or epidemiology mentioned in the introduction.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for the main results table despite averaging over 5 graph instances in some settings, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported differences, especially in closer comparisons (e.g., CauScale vs SDCD on NN non-additive data).

Causal sufficiency is assumed throughout (per Section 3), unlike FCI which handles latent confounders; this restricts applicability relative to some baselines, and the limitation is not explicitly discussed in the main text or impact statement beyond a general caveat about data quality.

Key hyperparameters of the reduction unit (reduction factor r, frequency k) appear tuned to specific values (B=10, k=2, r=2) without a systematic ablation across the full range of these values on the main training distribution, leaving their sensitivity somewhat unclear.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: existing pretraining-based methods (e.g., AVICI) scale poorly to large graphs in both time and memory. The paper offers a coherent set of architectural remedies (reduction unit, tied attention, two-stream data-graph blocks) targeted directly at this problem.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple axes: varying graph sizes (10 to 1000 nodes), causal mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), graph topologies (ER, SF, SBM), semi-synthetic GRN data (SERGIO), and OOD settings for graph structure, noise distribution, and mechanism function.

Strong quantitative improvements are demonstrated: near state-of-the-art mAP/AUC on in-distribution data, competitive OOD performance, and substantial (4x-13,000x) inference speedups, plus successful training/inference at scales (500-1000 nodes) where AVICI fails due to memory.

Thorough set of ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component: reduction unit vs. none, graph stream vs. graph prior removal, tied vs. vanilla attention, decomposed vs. vanilla prediction head, and pooling strategy choice — these convincingly support the design decisions.

Additional robustness analyses (latent confounders via node hiding, sensitivity to graph-prior sample size, sample-size scaling, pure observational data) go beyond a minimal evaluation and probe practical failure modes.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility appendix: hyperparameters, training schedule, hardware, baseline implementation details, and theoretical FLOP/memory complexity derivations are provided.
Honest limitations discussion (no real-world data, reliance on simulated training distribution) and an appropriate impact statement cautioning against blind trust in predicted graphs.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: tied attention weights are directly adopted from Rao et al. (2021, MSA Transformer), the decomposed prediction head is adopted from Wu et al. (2025, SEA), and the two-stream data/graph architecture closely follows the general paradigm of AVICI/SEA. The main new element is the reduction unit, which is essentially average pooling over the sample dimension between blocks — a relatively simple mechanism, though its combination with the rest of the pipeline is engineered carefully.

The claim of being 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale' understates that AVICI and SEA already establish the amortized/pretraining paradigm; the contribution is better framed as improving efficiency of an existing paradigm rather than pioneering it.

AVICI is evaluated using pretrained checkpoints rather than retrained on the same data as CauScale (due to its own OOM issues), which could bias comparisons since AVICI never saw the larger-scale training distribution CauScale uses; this makes some head-to-head accuracy comparisons less controlled.

Performance degrades substantially in compounded OOD settings (e.g., 18.9% mAP for polynomial mechanism at n=1000), and the model requires an ad hoc post-hoc cycle-breaking heuristic to guarantee acyclicity outside the training distribution, indicating the architecture does not intrinsically guarantee valid DAG outputs.

Evaluation is entirely on synthetic and semi-synthetic (SERGIO-simulated) data; there is no evaluation on any real observational dataset, which is an important gap for a paper motivated by real-world scientific/bioinformatics applications, even though this is acknowledged as a limitation.

Some headline efficiency claims (e.g., 13,000x speedup over NOTEARS) compare an amortized method against a non-amortized, per-dataset optimization baseline, which is an expected and somewhat unfair comparison inherent to the amortized-vs-non-amortized distinction rather than a novel efficiency insight specific to CauScale's design.

Statistical robustness of the main results is limited by only 5 independent test graphs per setting (with correspondingly large standard deviations reported in the appendix, e.g., ±199.5 SHD for n=1000 linear), which somewhat weakens the strength of the reported averages, especially for OOD settings.
No code or artifact release is directly visible/confirmed in the paper body (a project page is referenced but redacted for anonymity), leaving full reproducibility contingent on future release.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important bottleneck in amortized causal discovery: time and memory scaling with the number of variables, which is a known limitation of prior methods like AVICI.

The architectural ideas (axial-attention reduction unit over the observation dimension, tied/shared attention weights across axes, and a two-stream data/graph design with a data2graph distillation module) are reasonably well motivated and clearly described with accompanying FLOP- and memory-complexity derivations (Sections 4.6, Appendix E).

Broad empirical evaluation across synthetic SCMs (linear, additive/non-additive NN, OOD sigmoid/polynomial mechanisms) and a semi-synthetic single-cell GRN benchmark, with multiple metrics (mAP, SHD, AUC, OA, cyclicity, AID family).

Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of the reduction unit, graph stream/prior, tied attention vs. vanilla attention, prediction head design, and pooling strategy, plus auxiliary robustness studies (latent confounders, graph-prior sample size, inference sample-size sensitivity).

Reports substantial inference speedups (up to ~13,000x vs. NOTEARS, ~4x vs. AVICI) and demonstrates training feasibility at 500-node graphs where AVICI reportedly runs out of memory, which if correct is a meaningful practical gain.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: hyperparameters, baseline implementation details, data-generation procedures, and hardware specifications are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: No evaluation on real-world observational datasets; all experiments are on synthetic SCM data and a semi-synthetic simulator (SERGIO-GRN). Given that amortized causal discovery methods are trained on simulated distributions, the central claim of practical usefulness for 'scientific AI and data analysis' is not substantiated by any genuine real-data benchmark, and the paper itself concedes this limitation without addressing it empirically.

The claimed OOD generalization is weak in the settings that matter most: performance drops sharply for OOD mechanisms at large scale (e.g., 18.9% mAP, SHD std of ~2975 on n=1000 polynomial), and the model produces cyclic graphs requiring a post-hoc heuristic cycle-breaking fix in these harder regimes, undermining the paper's headline scalability/accuracy claims (99.6%/84.4% mAP figures in the abstract are not representative of the harder OOD large-graph settings reported later).

Baseline comparison fairness is questionable: AVICI is evaluated using only a pretrained checkpoint (because training it caused OOM), while CauScale is trained with a large, dedicated compute budget (8×H200 GPUs, ~40-47 GPU-hours per stage) directly on the matched training distributions; this asymmetry in training data/compute makes the large reported speed and accuracy gaps only partially attributable to the proposed architecture.

The core technical novelty is incremental/combinatorial: tied attention is directly adopted from Rao et al. (2021) MSA Transformer, average-pooling-based sequence reduction is a standard technique, and the two-stream/data-graph fusion design is architecturally similar to existing graph-neural or dual-stream causal discovery pipelines (e.g., SEA, AVICI). The main contribution is engineering these components together for causal discovery rather than introducing a fundamentally new causal-discovery principle.

Statistical robustness of reported numbers is limited: most test settings average over only 5 independent graphs, and some reported standard deviations are extremely large relative to the mean (e.g., SHD of 3985±2975 for n=1000 polynomial), raising concern about the reliability of point-estimate comparisons and whether the reported superiority is robust.

The method assumes causal sufficiency as a core modeling assumption (Section 3), and while a post hoc confounder-robustness experiment is included, it only simulates confounding via node removal rather than genuinely testing the model under the causal-sufficiency violation it was not trained to handle, so the claims of robustness are limited in scope.

The statistical graph prior (inverse covariance) is a purely linear/Gaussian quantity, yet the paper demonstrates substantial gains from using it even for nonlinear mechanisms without a clear theoretical justification for why this signal remains informative, leaving the role of the prior under nonlinearity insufficiently analyzed.

The efficiency framing (emphasizing fast inference) somewhat obscures that the training cost is itself very large (two-stage training with up to ~40 GPU-hours per stage on 8 high-end GPUs), which is not clearly contextualized against the amortized training costs of baselines like SEA or AVICI, making the overall efficiency narrative incomplete.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: scaling amortized causal discovery to much larger graphs than prior neural methods (AVICI, SEA), which currently suffer from severe memory/time bottlenecks.

Technically sound architectural contributions: the reduction unit (progressive compression along the observation axis) and tied attention weights (adapted from MSA Transformer) are well justified both intuitively and with rigorous FLOP/memory complexity analysis (Sections 4.6, Appendix E) showing concrete asymptotic savings.

The two-stream data-graph block design is a sensible way to inject graph priors and mitigate information loss from compression, and ablations (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5) convincingly isolate the contribution of each component (reduction unit, graph stream, graph prior, tied attention, prediction head).

Extensive empirical evaluation across many axes: multiple causal mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), multiple graph generators (ER, SF, SBM), varying graph sizes (10 to 1000 nodes), semi-synthetic SERGIO-GRN data, and 8 evaluation metrics (SHD, mAP, AUC, OA, Cyclicity, AID family), which is considerably more thorough than typical causal-discovery papers.

Strong and consistent empirical gains: near-saturating in-distribution accuracy (99.6% mAP), substantial out-of-distribution generalization advantage over baselines, and dramatic inference speedups (4x-13,000x) with much lower memory footprint (successfully scales to 500-node training and 1000-node inference where AVICI fails via OOM).

Good supplementary analyses: robustness to latent confounders, sensitivity to graph-prior estimation error, sample-size scaling behavior, and performance under pure observational (non-interventional) data, which collectively strengthen confidence in practical applicability.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information: hyperparameters, training compute/time, baseline implementation details, and data generation protocols are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: No evaluation on real-world observational causal discovery benchmarks (e.g., bnlearn networks, Sachs protein data) — all reported results are on synthetic or semi-synthetic simulated data, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which still limits confidence that gains transfer to messier real data.

Performance degrades substantially in OOD settings that combine both unseen graph scale and unseen causal mechanism (e.g., polynomial at n=1000: 18.9% mAP, with the paper itself acknowledging large cycle counts and needing cycle-breaking as a post-hoc fix), suggesting the strong headline numbers are somewhat dependent on in-distribution assumptions about graph size/mechanism at training time.

The reduction unit's effect on accuracy at smaller graph sizes (e.g., n=100) is attributed partly to 'training efficiency' rather than a clean ablation isolating this confound (same compute budget, same data), making the claim that reduction improves accuracy (rather than just efficiency) less rigorously supported.

AVICI is evaluated via pretrained checkpoints rather than retrained on the same training distribution/budget as CauScale for most comparisons (since AVICI OOMs on larger graphs), which somewhat complicates a fully controlled, apples-to-apples comparison, although this limitation is reasonably disclosed.

Some ablations (attention shape/output head, pooling strategy) are run only on small subsets of node counts (n ≤ 100 or ≤50), leaving open whether these architectural choices hold at the large scales that are the paper's central selling point.

The method still assumes causal sufficiency (no unobserved confounders) per the preliminaries, yet the paper markets itself as targeting general 'scientific AI' applications where confounding is common; the confounder-robustness experiment (Section 5.6) is a reasonable step but uses a simplified heuristic (top-out-degree node removal) rather than a more principled latent-confounder evaluation.

Presentation could be improved in places — e.g., dense efficiency-analysis equations in the main text (Section 4.6) might be better placed in the appendix to leave more room for deeper discussion of accuracy-efficiency trade-offs and failure modes in the main paper.
